parts: Tools for decorating a cake: grease proof paper (to line a cake base or make a piping bag), piping bags of canvas or nylon, scissors, nozzles of different shapes, brushes, palette knife (to smoothen icing), sharp knife (to slice the cake into two halves), rolling pin, flower or biscuit cutters, cake stand or turntable, cake pillars (for two or three tiered cakes), cooling rack, cake combs (for a decorative touch) and cake decorations. The basic process has four steps: (1) preparing a cake base (thick cardboard slightly bigger than the cake, 1 inch bigger in diameter for a round cake and 1/2 inch on each side for a square cake, covered with aluminium foil, so that the cake is easy to handle and hygienic; the cake is placed upside down for a smooth top), (2) giving a filling (cut the cake horizontally into two equal layers), (3) applying icing on the top and sides with a palette knife and combing the sides, and (4) piping and decoration with a piping bag and nozzles (star, flower, ribbon). A piping bag can be made from a 40 cm x 25 cm rectangle of grease proof paper folded into a cone with the tip cut so that the nozzle can be inserted from inside.

Butter icing is the most commonly used icing (about 50% of cakes) because it needs comparatively less skill, is easy to handle and can be stored at room temperature for about a fortnight in a well ventilated room; it hardens in the refrigerator, so bring it back to room temperature before use. It is made by creaming saltless butter or margarine with an equal weight of icing sugar (1:1) until light and fluffy; colour is added a drop at a time so that you can stop when the desired intensity is reached. Variations: chocolate, coffee, lemon or orange, vanilla and walnut butter icing. Cream icing is made from chilled fresh cream, sugar (20% of the cream) and vanilla essence, beaten over a bed of ice; if overbeaten the cream curdles and butter separates, if under-beaten it stays thin and does not hold the design. The test: lift the beater; if the cream does not fall off it, the icing is ready. A cake decorated with cream icing can be stored in a refrigerator for a maximum of two days, after which the cream is likely to turn sour.
Marzipan, royal icing, glace icing, fondant and chocolate icing

Marzipan is a clay like paste made out of ground almonds and a mixture of sugars (almonds, castor sugar, icing sugar, lemon juice, almond flavour and egg). It is used to cover cakes for a smooth, flat surface before royal icing is applied. It tends to be oily and crumbly, so avoid over-kneading, which releases oil and makes it sticky; being uncooked, it should not be stored for more than 3 days. To apply: brush the cake with apricot jam (other jams spoil the flavour), roll out the marzipan to 5 mm, cover the top and then the sides, and smooth the joins with a palette knife. Royal icing gives a royal touch to wedding cakes and has a shiny look; egg whites and sieved icing sugar are beaten with a fork (not an egg beater) in a grease free, non-plastic bowl; liquid colours are preferred; it has a low keeping quality, so use it fresh; it is ready when it stands in a peak. Glace icing is quickly made from icing sugar and warm water with no cooking, is suitable for small cakes and iced tea fancies and sets very quickly so should be used immediately. Fondant icing is made by boiling sugar, water and liquid glucose to 240 F (160 C), cooling, working to a smooth white mass; it is stored in a sealed container in a fridge for about four weeks, is used for icing cakes and making cake decorations and has a softer, more moulded look. Chocolate icing is a smooth glossy icing made by heating chocolate gently with cream, cooling until it coats a spoon and pouring over the cake.
